assertions: dexVariables2 BITS_DEX_V2_VARIABLES2_FETCH_DYNAMIC_FEE_FLAG == 1 (i.e. controller-driven dynamic fee enabled for this pool)
dexKey.controller is set to the malicious-controller contract
feeVersion == 1 (dynamic fee path) so the controller call branch is reachable
Pool has non-zero active liquidity and at least one resting LP position whose fees are accrued via feeGrowthGlobalX102
setup_calls: Admin (or governance) sets dexKey.controller = MaliciousController and flips fetchDynamicFee flag ON (the only on-chain prerequisite the attack relies on)
Honest LPs add liquidity expecting the controller-set dynamic fee to compensate them during volatility

post_vuln_state.custom_assertion: assertEq(v_.constantLpFee, 0); // a swapper paid zero LP fee while controller's override flag was active

attack_steps: Controller deploys a contract whose fetchDynamicFeeForSwapIn / fetchDynamicFeeForSwapOut returns abi.encode(uint256(0), true) — always 64 bytes, always succeeds.

Any swapper (msg.sender != controller) triggers the controller call at swapModuleInternals.sol L70-L83. success_ == true, returnData_.length == 64, fetchedDynamicFee_ = 0 (NOT > X16, so the bound check at L79 does not flip overrideDynamicFee_ back to false).
Branch at L86 takes overrideDynamicFee_ == true; v_.isConstantLpFee = true; v_.constantLpFee = fetchedDynamicFee_ = 0.

Swap proceeds with stepLpFeeRaw_ accrual at L156-L159 short-circuited by `if (... && v_.constantLpFee > 0)` — so feeGrowthGlobal0X102 / feeGrowthGlobal1X102 receive no LP-fee credit despite real swap volume passing through the active range.

Repeat continuously: LPs receive ZERO fees. Controller can be set to any contract by admin, including via governance compromise; if admin trust is the assumed boundary, this is a *trust upgrade* finding — the controller has *unbounded LP-fee-zero* power even on swaps it does not initiate, going beyond a normal `setFee` admin function which would at least require a tx and emit an event. Override happens silently per-swap.

Symmetric griefing: returning (X16, true) — exactly 65535 (~6.55%) — passes the L79 bound (only >X16 is rejected, equality is accepted) and combined with maximum protocol_cut_fee makes nearly every swap revert in slippage checks for honest users.
preconditions: The controller address is mutable per dexKey (per d1/d2/d3/d4 admin module)
fetchDynamicFee flag is enabled on the pool

triage.drop_reason: Verification not performed in this iteration (full mainnet-fork PoC against deployed FluidDexV2 stack would consume the entire 15-iteration budget). Rationale: the controller hook at swapModuleInternals.sol L70-L83 has only an UPPER bound (`fetchedDynamicFee_ > X16` rejects), with no LOWER bound and no governance-time-lock around the override. The override is silent and per-swap. Combined with the controller being a *normal address* (not a special timelocked role) and the fetchDynamicFee flag being a single bit in dexVariables2, a compromised or malicious-by-design controller can drain LP fee revenue without any visible event. The intended `_validateLPFee` check at _initialize is bypassed because override does not flow through that path. KG seed: closest analog is the Uniswap-v4 hook abuse class — hooks that can return arbitrary fee values without floor checks. MCGA: dexCallback / fetchDynamicFeeForSwapIn ranks high in external-call sink density on this codebase. Severity is medium if controller is admin-trusted (LP-fee theft is direct economic loss to LPs); high if any non-admin path can set the controller.

deployments: addr:<FluidDexV2D3 or D4 instance with smart-debt enabled>
deploy:AttackerWrapper that loops add/remove with same amounts

assertions: Pool exists with isSmartDebt=true (round-up branch active in _addLiquidity)
Attacker can add and remove liquidity in the same range without slippage limits hindering the dust
tickLower and tickUpper straddle currentTick so liquidity is 'active' (otherwise add/remove is 1-token only and the asymmetry is harder to monetize)
setup_calls: Attacker calls _addLiquidity with amount0DesiredRaw_, amount1DesiredRaw_ that produce a non-trivial liquidity number around the rounding boundary
Then immediately _removeLiquidity with the same amounts

post_vuln_state.custom_assertion: assertGt(positionData_.liquidity_after_round_trip, 0); // dust accumulates after add+remove of identical token amounts

attack_steps: Attacker deposits (amount0, amount1) into smart-debt branch. _addLiquidity rounds liquidityIncreaseRaw_ UP via `(L * ROUNDING_FACTOR_PLUS_ONE) / ROUNDING_FACTOR + 1` (L41) — protocol pays the attacker MORE liquidity than the canonical Uniswap math would produce.
On _removeLiquidity (L231-L237) the protocol calls `LA.getLiquidityForAmounts(...)` directly with NO matching round-up/round-down adjustment, so liquidityDecreaseRaw_ is the raw, un-rounded amount.

Net effect of identical-amount round trip: position retains `(rounded_up_add - raw_remove)` liquidity, paid for by the asymmetry — i.e., the protocol overcounted on add but undercounted on remove. The leftover dust is effectively free liquidity.

Repeat thousands of times in a single tx (gas-bounded only). Each iteration leaks ~ROUNDING_FACTOR_PLUS_ONE/ROUNDING_FACTOR ratio dust into attacker's position. Once the position is meaningful, withdraw at a different price (or burn fee growth) for profit.

Symmetric inverse for isSmartCollateral=true (L37-L38): add rounds DOWN, remove uses raw — attacker gets back MORE tokens than they put in via remove because liquidityDecreaseRaw_ is raw-computed from the same desired amounts but the position holds the rounded-down liquidity. Exact direction of the leak depends on the (price, range, amounts) tuple.
preconditions: Attacker can call user-facing add/remove liquidity within a single tx (no time-locks, no per-position cooldowns)
No fee on add or remove that dominates the rounding dust
Position is identified by `keccak256(abi.encode(msg.sender, tickLower, tickUpper, positionSalt))` so the attacker can target exactly the same position

triage.drop_reason: Verification not performed in this iteration. Rationale: the round-up at userModuleInternals.sol L40-L42 is asymmetric with the lack-of-round at L231-L237. The comment at L36 says 'protocol is on the winning side' — but that's only true if the OPPOSITE rounding is applied at remove. Code does not. The dust per round-trip is small (1 part in ROUNDING_FACTOR), but compoundable in a single transaction since there are no rate limits between add and remove of the same position. Whether net profit > gas is sensitive to the exact ROUNDING_FACTOR (need to grep constantVariables.sol — likely 1e6 or 1e9). MCGA: _addLiquidity / _removeLiquidity rank in the top-5 unchecked-arith sink density for dexV2. KG seed: pattern resembles the Cream Finance and Hundred-Finance round-trip dust drains; specifically the mDAI exploit (DeFiHackLabs 2022-04-27) where rounding asymmetry between mint/burn enabled drain via repeated calls. Severity is medium if ROUNDING_FACTOR is large enough that gas is amortized; low otherwise.

deployments: addr:<FluidDexV2D3 or D4 instance with fetchDynamicFee flag ON>
deploy:GriefingController whose fetchDynamicFeeForSwapIn always reverts OR returns mismatched data

assertions: fetchDynamicFee flag ON on the pool
Pool's controller is set (governance attack vector OR one-time admin setup error)
feeVersion == 1 OR feeVersion == 0 — both reach the controller call as long as the flag bit is on
setup_calls: Controller is configured as a contract that consumes >200K gas in fetchDynamicFeeForSwapIn (e.g., loops over a large storage array, or calls another contract)

post_vuln_state.custom_assertion: assertEq(v_.constantLpFee, default_fee_NOT_dynamic_fee); // controller's intended dynamic fee was silently dropped

attack_steps: Step 1 — silent fail-open. The dex calls `controller.call{gas: 200000}(...)` (L73). On out-of-gas, success_ == false, override is skipped, and v_.constantLpFee falls back to (a) static lpFee at L91 if feeVersion==0, or (b) dynamic fee from `_computeSwapStepForSwapInWithDynamicFee` at L162 if feeVersion==1.

Step 2 — controller-set dynamic fee never applies. If the controller is *meant* to raise fees during a price-manipulation event (e.g., return higher-than-baseline fee when sqrtPriceX96 deviates from oracle), an attacker can pad calldata with extra non-zero data or simply submit during a high-base-fee block to make the call OOG. The fall-through fee is the LOWER static one. The attacker swaps cheaply during exactly the moment the controller wanted to penalize swaps.

Step 3 — alternate path: malicious controller deliberately returns mismatched return-data length (e.g., 96 bytes by encoding (uint256, bool, uint256)). L77 `success_ && returnData_.length == 64` rejects the override, falling back to default. Now controller can selectively decline to override (whitelist its own swaps but force-reject for others) — but since msg.sender==controller is already a special-case fast-path at L70, the relevant case is: controller is NOT msg.sender, controller wants to GIVE this swapper a discount, but the dex's return-length check rejects ABI-non-canonical encodings.

Step 4 — economic impact. During a multi-block volatility window, attacker stacks N swaps each of size approaching the active liquidity. Each swap pays the lower fallback fee instead of the controller-set surge fee. Aggregate LP loss = N * size * (surge_fee - fallback_fee) which for fee_diff = 5% and size = $1M is $50K per swap.
preconditions: Controller logic depends on >200K gas to compute the surge fee (e.g., reads from a TWAP, calls Chainlink, walks a pricing table)
Attacker can trigger swaps adjacent to the high-cost code path (mempool front-run + access-list manipulation increases base call gas)

triage.drop_reason: Verification not performed in this iteration. Rationale: the silent fail-open semantics at swapModuleInternals.sol L82-L83 is intentional ('On failure or wrong return data size, use default values'). This is a valid design choice IF the controller is required to be gas-bounded; the comment at L72 claims '200K is sufficient for any reasonable fee calculation'. But Chainlink AggregatorV3 + uniswap TWAP read + Solidity-level math regularly cumulates >150K gas, leaving very little headroom; under a 1559 high-base-fee block, the L1 sub-call gas accounting can OOG inside the controller before the fee is computed. KG seed: matches the known fail-open class on Compound oracle and the Synthetix-pricer staleness pattern — protocols that fall back to a *cheaper* default rather than reverting create an attacker-chosen-fail surface. MCGA: ranks #4 by external-call sink density. Severity depends on whether controller-set surge fees are part of intended LP protection mechanism — if yes, this is medium; if controllers are only used for additive special-case discounts, this is informational.
